strengths: Well-motivated problem: Clear articulation of how GRPO's scalar advantage discards critical spatial structure in visual content, with concrete examples demonstrating the limitation

Comprehensive experimental validation: Extensive evaluation on both image and video generation with multiple reward models, out-of-domain testing, and thorough ablation studies examining four key components
Consistent improvements: Across all benchmarks and variants, ViPO shows improvements over both vanilla GRPO and DanceGRPO, with particularly strong out-of-domain generalization
Practical and lightweight design: Simple approach using standard techniques (PCA + pretrained features), fully compatible with existing GRPO pipelines, no dense annotations required
Robust ablation methodology: Systematic validation of design choices (allocation map necessity, aggregation strategy, component count, smoothing effects) with clear performance trends
Convincing qualitative evidence: High-quality visual examples (Figures 3-5) demonstrating improvements in coherence, realism, semantic fidelity, and robustness to degenerate rewards
Flexible backbone support: Demonstrates generality by testing with DINO, SAM, and ResNet, with principled selection based on performance
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: Core contribution—applying PCA to pretrained features for spatial weighting—combines existing techniques without substantial methodological innovation; feels incremental rather than conceptual

Lack of theoretical justification: No principled explanation for why PCA components should correspond to perceptually important regions; the connection between explained variance and perceptual importance is assumed but never validated

Incomplete allocation map analysis: Critical visualizations absent from main paper; without seeing allocation maps, cannot verify they capture meaningful semantic structure or understand what components represent
Modest quantitative improvements: Image improvements of 3.7% (HPSv2.1), out-of-domain results mixed (PickScore shows -0.8% on DINO variant); lacking statistical significance testing
Backbone selection dependency: Large performance variance across backbones (DINO: 0.3321 vs SAM: 0.3219); minimal investigation into why SAM fails or how to select backbones for new domains
Missing computational cost analysis: No discussion of training time, memory overhead, or wall-clock cost despite adding backbone inference and PCA at each GRPO step; critical for practitioners
Technical detail gaps: Unclear how allocation maps are computed/aligned across diffusion steps, whether they're static or dynamic, and how spatio-temporal maps are constructed for video
Limited experimental scope: Only two base models tested; 3200 image and 1000 video test prompts; video training uses downsampled resolution; no evaluation on other recent generative models

Inconsistent out-of-domain generalization: PickScore shows marginal/negative gains while other metrics improve; semantic alignment for video marginally improves (0.35% on VBench); unclear how method generalizes
Generalization concerns: Dependence on pretrained backbone choice and unclear applicability to other reward models, visual tasks, or generation paradigms beyond text-to-image/video
Redness reward experiment limitations: Artificial hand-crafted reward doesn't reflect realistic adversarial scenarios; would benefit from more diverse degenerate rewards
Limited failure case analysis: SAM variant underperforms with minimal investigation; no discussion of when spatial allocation might hurt or which prompt/content types cause failures
Reproducibility barriers: Code release not mentioned; extreme computational requirements (32 H100s for video) limit reproduction; key implementation details in supplementary material
Missing baseline comparisons: No comparison with simpler alternatives (direct attention maps, learned masks, saliency-based weighting) or other spatial credit assignment approaches

strengths: Well-motivated problem identifying a genuine limitation of GRPO for visual generation—treating entire images/videos as scalar values ignores spatial structure and fine-grained perceptual cues
Comprehensive experimental validation across dual modalities (images and videos), multiple reward models, out-of-domain generalization, and several backbone choices with detailed ablation studies

Compelling evidence of method effectiveness through the redness reward experiment (Figure 5), demonstrating that ViPO preserves semantic integrity under adversarial rewards, suggesting robustness benefits beyond marginal gains
Practical efficiency with minimal computational overhead (1-4.8% step time increase, <4.5% memory) making the approach readily adoptable into existing GRPO pipelines
Clear presentation with effective visualizations (particularly Figures 1-2) communicating core intuitions, and logical progression from motivation through method to results
Consistent improvements across both in-domain and out-of-domain metrics on both image and video generation tasks
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the core contribution—multiplying advantages by spatial weighting maps—is straightforward; PSM uses standard techniques (PCA, channel weighting) without methodological innovation

Insufficient theoretical justification for why multiplying by spatial maps improves optimization; claims about preventing gradient interference lack rigorous analysis, and no formal study of effects on GRPO convergence properties
Modest quantitative improvements (3.7% for FLUX HPSv2.1, 14.8% for Wan2.1 VQ) that are consistent but not dramatic, raising questions about practical significance
Core mechanism remains unclear: paper demonstrates improvements but provides limited insight into whether gains stem from gradient stabilization, artifact suppression, or focus on semantic regions

Under-justified design choices for allocation maps: PCA selection lacks comparison to alternatives; K=3 appears arbitrary with metric-dependent performance; different backbones produce drastically different maps without clear principled justification for which is 'correct'

No validation that allocation maps capture actual human visual importance: claims about DINOv2 alignment with human preference are unsupported; backbone sensitivity suggests method may capture arbitrary feature representations rather than true perceptual importance

Limited baseline comparisons: only compared against vanilla GRPO through DanceGRPO; no comparison with other structured-feedback approaches (saliency weighting, attention-based, learned weighting) despite their mention in related work

Evaluation gaps: based on automated metrics without human studies; qualitative examples appear cherry-picked; 'out-of-domain' uses different reward models, not true distribution shift; no statistical significance testing or confidence intervals
Unclear method semantics: Equation 8's claim that multiplying by spatially varying M(p) 'maintains consistent optimization direction' contradicts the assertion that it creates region-specific updates

Reproducibility concerns: code unavailable; design choices (ResNet layer, σ=1, K=3) appear post-hoc from ablations; sensitivity to initialization and randomness not discussed; limited justification for layer-selection in CNN backbone

strengths: Clear problem formulation: paper identifies and articulates a genuine limitation of GRPO for visual generation—the spatial credit assignment problem from using scalar advantages for spatially-rich content like images and videos.

Comprehensive experimental validation across both image (FLUX.1-dev with HPSv2.1/PickScore/ImageReward) and video (Wan2.1 with VideoAlign/VBench) benchmarks with both in-domain and out-of-domain generalization testing.
Practical design with minimal overhead (1-4.8% training time, <4.5% memory) and full compatibility with existing GRPO pipelines, making it readily adoptable.

Thorough ablation studies systematically examining allocation map necessity, aggregation strategies, PCA component count, and smoothing effects, demonstrating benefits come from semantic structure rather than pixel-wise decomposition alone.
Consistent improvements across multiple metrics and datasets, with particularly strong results on video generation (14.8% VQ, 33.3% MQ improvement), indicating general effectiveness of the approach.
Robustness analysis via redness reward experiment (Section 4.3) shows ViPO better preserves semantic integrity under adversarial reward signals, suggesting improved optimization stability.

Well-executed research with clear motivation, clean presentation, interpretable visualizations of allocation maps, and thorough supplementary material detailing PSM computation and additional results.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: the core contribution is relatively straightforward (multiplying scalar advantages by spatial maps via PCA of pretrained features), representing an incremental combination of existing techniques rather than a fundamentally new idea.

Lack of theoretical analysis: no justification for why element-wise multiplication of allocation maps with advantages solves credit assignment better than alternatives; missing analysis of gradient flow effects and properties of M(p) that enable effectiveness.

Fixed (non-learned) allocation maps present a conceptual limitation: maps are deterministic outputs computed before RL training and cannot adapt to specific reward models or policy changes, limiting true credit assignment versus providing implicit regularization.

Modest empirical improvements without statistical significance testing: image generation gains ~3.7% (HPSv2.1), out-of-domain results inconsistent across metrics (PickScore varies 22.54-22.85), and no confidence intervals or significance tests provided to establish practical meaningfulness.

Incomplete backbone analysis: SAM significantly underperforms DINOv2, undermining claims of architecture-agnosticism; paper attributes underperformance to 'low-level content' without deeper investigation into which backbone properties are essential.

Missing key comparisons: no evaluation against other spatial weighting schemes (learned masks, saliency maps, attention), other GRPO variants (MixGRPO mentioned but not compared), or alternative RL approaches for visual generation.

Allocation map validation relies primarily on qualitative visual inspection; no rigorous evaluation that extracted maps align with human-defined important regions, and examples show SAM assigns high weights to background regions without clear explanation.
Video implementation underspecified: spatio-temporal volume construction and per-frame temporal alignment described vaguely in main paper with minimal supplementary details, limiting reproducibility.

Generalization claims overstated: paper claims 'enhanced generalization' but out-of-domain results are inconsistent (strong on ImageReward, variable on PickScore), not supporting universally strong generalization.

Missing analyses: no investigation of why variance-weighted PCA aggregation outperforms simple averaging (suggesting learned weighting might work better), limited analysis across prompt types/styles, and no investigation of potential mismatch between pretrained feature saliency and reward signal values.
